{{Short description|none}}
{{Infobox place demographics|place=[[Penang]]|size_of_population=1,740,405 (2020){{my10|2020kf}}|density=1,659/km2{{my10|2020kf}}|birth=11.3 births/1,000 population (2020)<ref name="DOSMVitalStats"/>|death=6.1 deaths/1,000 population (2020)<ref name="DOSMVitalStats"/>|life=74.2 years (2020)<ref name="DOSMVitalStats"/>|life_male=72.0 years (2020)<ref name="DOSMVitalStats"/>|life_female=76.7 years (2020)<ref name="DOSMVitalStats"/>|fertility=1.3 (2020)<ref name="DOSMVitalStats"/>|age_0–14_years=20.1%|age_15-64_years=73.3%|age_65_years=6.6%|major_ethnic=[[Penangite Chinese|Chinese]], [[Malaysian Malays|Malay]], [[Malaysians of Indian descent in Penang|Indians]], [[Peranakan Chinese|Peranakans]], [[Kristang people|Eurasians]], [[Malaysian Siamese|Siamese]]|minor_ethnic=<!-- language -->|official=[[Malay language|Malay]]|spoken=[[British English|English]], [[Malay language|Malay]], [[Penang Hokkien]], [[Malaysian Mandarin|Mandarin]], [[Tamil language|Tamil]]|growth=1.3% (2020){{my10|2020kf}}}}
'''[[Penang]]''' is a diverse multiethnic and multicultural society. Residents of the state are colloquially known as Penangites or "Penang-lang".<ref>{{Cite news |last=Opalyn Mok |date=19 August 2017 |title=Has Mandarin Replaced Hokkien in Penang? |url=https://www.malaymail.com/news/malaysia/2017/08/19/has-mandarin-replaced-hokkien-in-penang/1445715 |access-date=17 Dec 2023 |work=[[Malay Mail]]}}</ref> Traditionally regarded as a [[Penangite Chinese|Chinese]]-majority state, the [[Bumiputera (Malaysia)|''Bumiputera'']] population, which includes ethnic [[Malaysian Malays|Malays]], has reached parity with that of the Chinese in recent years.
 
{{As of|2020}}, the population of Penang stood at 1,740,405, growing by about 1.3% annually. 1,599,874, or 91.9%, were Malaysian citizens, while 140,531 were non-citizens. Ethnic Chinese, Malays and [[Malaysians of Indian descent in Penang|Indians]] cumulatively comprised nearly 91% of Penang's population.{{my10|2020kf}} Total fertility rate was 1.3 that year.<ref name="DOSMVitalStats">{{Cite journal |date=Oct 2023 |title=Vital Statistics Malaysia 2023 |journal=[[Department of Statistics Malaysia]] |issn=0127-466X}}</ref>
 
Penang has the highest population density of all Malaysian states at {{Convert|1659|/km2|abbr=on}}, as well as an urbanisation rate of 92.5%, the second highest after [[Selangor]].{{my10|2020kf}}<ref name="Malay Mail-2022">{{Cite news |date=23 Dec 2022 |title=Statistics Dept: Malaysia's Urbanisation Rate Tripled over Five Decades |url=https://www.malaymail.com/news/malaysia/2022/12/23/statistics-dept-malaysias-urbanisation-rate-tripled-over-five-decades/46783 |access-date=4 Dec 2023 |work=[[Malay Mail]]}}</ref> [[Seberang Perai]], Malaysia's third largest city, was home to over 54% of Penang's population, while [[George Town, Penang|George Town]] contained nearly 46%. George Town serves as the [[core city]] of the [[George Town Conurbation]], Malaysia's [[List of cities and towns in Malaysia by population#Largest metropolitan areas by population|second largest metropolitan area]], home to a population of over 2.84 million.{{my10|2020kf}}
 
[[Islam]] is the state's official religion, but [[Buddhism]], [[Hinduism]] and [[Christianity]] are cumulatively proscribed by over half of the state's population.{{my10|2020kf}}<ref name="Penang State Gov">{{Cite journal |title=Constitution of the State of Penang |url=https://dun.penang.gov.my/images/v25/Perlembagaan%20Negeri_VERSI%20BM_BI.pdf |journal=[[Government of Penang|Penang state government]] |archive-date=2024-03-09 |access-date=2024-08-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240309171727/https://dun.penang.gov.my/images/v25/Perlembagaan%20Negeri_VERSI%20BM_BI.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Within [[Peninsular Malaysia]], Penang is the only state with a non-Muslim majority.{{my10|2020kf}} While [[Malay language|Malay]] is the official language of Malaysia, [[British English|English]], [[Malaysian Mandarin|Mandarin]] and [[Tamil language|Tamil]] are also widely used within Penang.<ref name="Teresa Wai-20223">{{Cite journal |last=Teresa Wai |first=See Ong |date=May 2022 |title=Building Relationships with Community Members: Lessons Learnt from Fieldwork in Penang, Malaysia |url=https://repository.nie.edu.sg/server/api/core/bitstreams/57a48a8d-6fab-4c08-a012-5ad54c6fddc9/content |journal=[[Griffith University]]}}</ref> [[Penang Hokkien]], a variant of the [[Southern Min]] group of languages, remains the unofficial ''[[lingua franca]]'' in the state.<ref name="Ooi Kok Hin">{{Cite web |last=Ooi Kok Hin |first=Julia Tan |title=Penang Hokkien on Life Support |url=http://penangmonthly.com/article.aspx?pageid=7412&name=penang_hokkien_on_life_support |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170615140306/http://penangmonthly.com/article.aspx?pageid=7412&name=penang_hokkien_on_life_support |archive-date=15 June 2017 |access-date=2017-05-27 |website=Penang Monthly}}</ref>
 
The state's diversified economy has made it one of the major recipients of interstate migrants within Malaysia.<ref>{{Cite news |date=30 May 2017 |title=Migration report: Selangor, Penang Most Popular with Locals |url=http://www.freemalaysiatoday.com/category/nation/2017/05/30/migration-report-selangor-penang-most-popular-with-locals/ |access-date=3 July 2017 |work=[[Free Malaysia Today]]}}</ref> Between 2015 and 2016, Penang achieved the highest migration effectiveness ratio among Malaysian states. For every 100 Malaysians that migrated into and out of Penang, the state's population increased by 58 persons.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Christopher Tan |date=24 June 2017 |title=Penang Ranks Second in Influx of New Residents |url=http://www.thestar.com.my/news/nation/2017/06/24/penang-ranks-second-in-influx-of-new-residents/ |work=[[The Star (Malaysia)|The Star]]}}</ref><ref name="interstatemigrant2">{{Cite journal |date=26 May 2017 |title=Migration Survey Report 2016 |url=https://newss.statistics.gov.my/newss-portalx/ep/epFreeDownloadContentSearch.seam?cid=21562 |journal=[[Department of Statistics Malaysia]] |issn=0127-8924}}</ref> The bulk of the interstate immigrants came from [[Perak]], [[Selangor]], [[Kedah]], [[Johor]] and [[Kuala Lumpur]].<ref name="interstatemigrant2" />
 
== History ==
{{Historical populations|1881|190597|1891|231224|1901|247808|1911|270537|1921|292485|1931|340259|1947|446321|1957|572100|1970|776124|1980|954638|1991|1116801|2000|1313449|2010|1526324|2020|1740405|shading=off|source={{my10|2020kf}}<ref name="1921census">{{Cite book |url=https://statsdigital.stats.gov.my/Penerbitan/penerbitan/view?id=5bc68d0dd5bc73855e4aae59 |title=Population Census 1921 Vol. 1 |pages=18}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |date=Dec 2006 |title=Data siri masa banci penduduk dan perumahan, 1911-2000 |url=https://statsdigital.stats.gov.my/Penerbitan/penerbitan/view?id=5bc68d0dd5bc73855e4aae1d |journal=[[Department of Statistics Malaysia]] |location=[[Putrajaya]] |pages=4 |isbn=978-983-9044-29-4}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |date=Aug 2014 |title=Migration and population distribution 2010 |url=https://www.mycensus.gov.my/index.php/census-product/publication/census-2010/683-migration-and-population-distribution-2010 |journal=[[Department of Statistics Malaysia]] |location=[[Putrajaya]] |pages=12 |isbn=978-983-9044-86-7}}</ref>}}

[[Penang Island]] had been sparsely populated prior to the establishment of [[George Town, Penang|George Town]]. The first British visit to Penang in 1592 recorded no people on the island but did encounter a group of [[Orang Asli]] on the mainland.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lim |first=Teckwyn |date=2021 |title='Sixteen Naked Indians': First Contact between the British and the Orang Asli |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/article/842105 |journal=Journal of the Malaysian Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society |volume=94 |issue=2 |pages=27–42 |doi=10.1353/ras.2021.0025 |issn=2180-4338|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Founded as an entrepot by [[Francis Light]] in 1786, George Town quickly experienced population growth fueled by immigration from various parts of [[Asia]].<ref name="Lewis-2016">{{Cite book |last=Lewis |first=Su Lin |title=Cities in Motion: Urban Life and Cosmopolitanism in Southeast Asia, 1920–1940 |publisher=[[University of Cambridge]] |year=2016 |isbn=9781107108332}}</ref><ref name="Keat Gin-2015">{{Cite journal |last=Ooi |first=Keat Gin |author-link=Keat Gin Ooi |date=2015 |title=Disparate Identities: Penang from a Historical Perspective, 1780–1941 |url=http://web.usm.my/km/33(Supp.2)2015/km33s22015_03.pdf |url-status=live |journal=Kajian Malaysia – Journal of Malaysian Studies |publisher=[[Universiti Sains Malaysia]] |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=27–52 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170207031500/http://web.usm.my/km/33%28Supp.2%292015/km33s22015_03.pdf |archive-date=7 February 2017 |access-date=22 December 2023}}</ref> At the time of George Town's establishment, Elisha Trapaud, a member of Light's landing party, described that the island was inhabited by “58 people in Malay-style houses”.<ref name="Zhao-2018">{{Cite journal |last=Zhao |first=Long |date=2 December 2018 |title=The Townscape Evolution of Historic Port Settlement of George Town, Pulau Pinang, Malaysia |url=https://frsb.upm.edu.my/upload/dokumen/20181224115748artikel_09.pdf |url-status=live |journal=[[University of Putra Malaysia]] |volume=11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231218151505/https://frsb.upm.edu.my/upload/dokumen/20181224115748artikel_09.pdf |archive-date=18 December 2023 |access-date=18 December 2023}}</ref> Within two years, George Town's population reached 1,000, increasing to 12,000 by 1804.<ref name="Keat Gin-2015" />
 
An official census in 1881 showed that Penang had a population of 190,597, or about 45% of the [[Straits Settlements]]’ population. Penang continued to hold the majority of the Straits Settlements’ population until 1911, when Singapore's population surpassed Penang by 311,985 to 278,003. Within the settlement of George Town, [[Penangite Chinese|ethnic Chinese]] comprised nearly 63% of the population in 1911.<ref name="1921census" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite book |title=Contested Holy Cities: The Urban Dimension of Religious Conflicts |publisher=[[Taylor & Francis]] |year=2019 |isbn=9780429673849 |editor-last=Dumper |editor-first=Michael}}</ref> By 1921, the Chinese population of Penang outstripped that of the Malays by 135,288 to 110,382.<ref name="1921census"/>
 
By the time [[Federation of Malaya|Malaya]] gained independence in 1957, Penang held a population of more than half a million.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=11 Jul 1959 |title=1957 population census report no. 3: State of Penang |url=https://statsdigital.stats.gov.my/Penerbitan/penerbitan/view?id=5bc68d0dd5bc73855e4aae22 |journal=Department of Statistics, Federation of Malaya |location=[[Kuala Lumpur]] |pages=4–6 |via=[[Department of Statistics Malaysia]]}}</ref> By 1991, Penang's population had exceeded one million, with mainland [[Seberang Perai]] overtaking Penang Island in population at the same time.<ref name="census1991">{{Cite journal |last=Khoo |first=Soo Gim |date=Feb 1995 |title=Population and housing census of Malaysia 1991: General report of the population census |url=https://statsdigital.stats.gov.my/Penerbitan/penerbitan/view?id=5bc68d0dd5bc73855e4aadf4 |journal=[[Department of Statistics Malaysia]] |location=[[Kuala Lumpur]] |volume=2 |pages=25 |issn=1394-3642}}</ref> However, the state's population growth had begun to slow since the 1970s. In 2020, annual population growth was at 1.3%, a reduction from 2.1% in 2010.{{my10|2020kf}}

== Population distribution ==
[[File:Map of population density in Penang.svg|thumb|Population density by subdivisions in Penang, derived from the 2020 census.<ref name="Department of Statistics Malaysia-2024" />]]
{{As of|2020}}, [[Seberang Perai]] contained a population of 946,092, or more than 54% of Penang's population. This also made Seberang Perai the [[List of cities and towns in Malaysia by population#Within defined boundaries|third largest city in Malaysia]], after [[Kuala Lumpur]] and [[Kajang]]. [[George Town, Penang|George Town]], the capital city of Penang, was home to 794,313 residents, or nearly 46% of the state's population. As George Town has a smaller land area, George Town's population density of {{Convert|2595.8|/km2|abbr=on}} was double that of Seberang Perai, which stood at {{Convert|1264.8|/km2|abbr=on}}.{{my10|2020kf}}
 
Within George Town, the areas with the highest density were [[Jelutong, Penang|Jelutong]], [[Ayer Itam]] and [[Tanjong Tokong]]. The [[Central George Town, Penang|city centre]] had a population density of {{Convert|6209|/km2|abbr=on}}. In Seberang Perai, Mukim 14 ([[Mak Mandin]]) recorded the highest population density, at {{Convert|7565|/km2|abbr=on}}.<ref name="Department of Statistics Malaysia-2024">{{Cite journal |date=February 2024 |title=MyCensus 2020: Mukim/Town/Pekan |journal=[[Department of Statistics Malaysia]] |isbn=9789672537069}}</ref>

==== Chinese ====
{{See also|Penangite Chinese}}
[[File:Chingay in George Town 2024.jpg|thumb|The [[Chingay parade]] is perceived as a major form of expression of the [[Penangite Chinese|Penang Chinese]] identity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Daniel Goh |first=P. S. |date=2011 |title=State carnivals and the subvention of multiculturalism in Singapore |url=https://ap5.fas.nus.edu.sg/fass/socgohd/bjos_1347.pdf |journal=[[National University of Singapore]] |page=120}}</ref>]]
Ethnic Chinese immigrants and traders had arrived on [[Penang Island]] in the years immediately after the founding of [[George Town, Penang|George Town]]. [[Francis Light]] noted in his diary on 18 July 1786, one day after his arrival on the island, that a group of Chinese led by a “Captain China” presented him with a gift of fishing nets. Chinese settlers began arriving at what is now the [[Central George Town, Penang|city centre]] and [[Tanjong Tokong]].<ref name="Zhao-2018" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Goh |first=Sang Seong |date=2015 |title=Penang Chinese Customs and Traditions |url=http://web.usm.my/km/33(Supp.2)2015/km33s22015_08.pdf |journal=Kajian Malaysia |publisher=[[Universiti Sains Malaysia]] |volume=33 |issue=Supp. 2}}</ref> Light regarded the Chinese as "a valuable acquisition" and "the only people of the [E]ast from whom a revenue [might] be raised without expense and extraordinary efforts of government". Under his successor [[George Alexander William Leith]], the Chinese population grew to approximately 6,000, with the wealthier class owning  "valuable estates, in land and houses", while artisans, labourers, fishermen and market. Gardeners commanded high wages because they were "laboriously good workmen".<ref name="Keat Gin-2015" />
 
The [[Peranakan Chinese]] soon evolved as an influential sub-group within George Town's Chinese community.<ref name="Keat Gin-20152">{{Cite journal |last=Keat Gin |first=Ooi |date=2015 |title=Disparate Identities: Penang from a Historical Perspective, 1780–1941 |url=http://web.usm.my/km/33(Supp.2)2015/km33s22015_03.pdf |url-status=live |journal=Kajian Malaysia – Journal of Malaysian Studies |publisher=[[Universiti Sains Malaysia]] |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=27–52 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170207031500/http://web.usm.my/km/33%28Supp.2%292015/km33s22015_03.pdf |archive-date=7 February 2017 |access-date=22 December 2023}}</ref><ref name="Koay-2016b2">{{Cite web |last=Koay |first=Su Lin |date=2016 |title=Penang: The Rebel State (Part One) |url=http://penangmonthly.com/article.aspx?pageid=2370&name=penang_the_rebel_state_part_one |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201034025/http://penangmonthly.com/article.aspx?pageid=2370&name=penang_the_rebel_state_part_one |archive-date=1 December 2017 |access-date=26 May 2017 |work=Penang Monthly}}</ref> Descendants of mixed Malay and Chinese ancestries who had inhabited the region for generations, the Peranakans adopted Malay socio-cultural traditions in terms of cuisine, attire and language, amalgamated with [[Chinese folk religion|Chinese beliefs]]. There was a distinct preference for English-medium education and consequently, the Peranakans were known as the "King's Chinese" for their loyalty to the [[Monarchy of the United Kingdom|British Crown]] rather than [[Qing dynasty|China]].<ref name="Jaime Koh-22">{{Cite web |last=Jaime Koh |title=Peranakan (Straits Chinese) Community |url=http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/infopedia/articles/SIP_2013-08-30_181745.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170604004706/http://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/infopedia/articles/SIP_2013-08-30_181745.html |archive-date=4 June 2017 |access-date=26 May 2017 |website=[[National Library Board]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Heaver |first=Stuart |date=10 May 2014 |title=High Society |url=https://www.scmp.com/magazines/post-magazine/article/1506517/high-society-preserving-peranakan-culture |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170603144323/http://www.scmp.com/magazines/post-magazine/article/1506517/high-society-preserving-peranakan-culture |archive-date=3 June 2017 |access-date=29 May 2017 |work=[[South China Morning Post]]}}</ref> They also retained significant influence in the city's commercial and societal spheres.<ref name="Jaime Koh-22" /><ref name="Koay-2016b2"/>
 
The Peranakans were distinct from waves of newer arrivals from China, known colloquially as “sin-kheh”. Originating from [[Fujian]] and [[Guangdong]] provinces, the “sin-kheh” were divided along dialect lines, establishing [[Kongsi|clan associations]] to assist new arrivals in accommodation, protection and employment. The [[Hoklo people|Hokkiens]] and the [[Teochew people|Teochews]] formed the bulk of the new arrivals, and dominated trade, real estate, large plantation-scale commercial agriculture, and retail shopkeeping. The [[Cantonese people|Cantonese]] arrived in smaller numbers, but were considered more hardy and robust, and they predominated as artisans and traders. Other dialect groups included the [[Hakka people|Hakkas]] and the [[Hainan people|Hainanese]].<ref name="Keat Gin-2015" /> The waves of Chinese immigration also created predominantly Chinese areas within George Town such as the [[Clan Jetties]], while in mainland Province Wellesley (now [[Seberang Perai]]), cash crop industries attracted Teochew planters to areas like [[Bukit Mertajam]], [[Bukit Tambun]] and [[Batu Kawan]].<ref name="Keat Gin-2015" /><ref name=":25">{{Cite journal |last=Chan |first=Wai Yeap |title=The History of Bukit Mertajam (1800-1957): From Agrarian Town to Central Hub of Northern Malaya |url=https://www.academia.edu/25915163 |journal=Penang Institute |via=[[Academia.edu]]}}</ref>

==== Malay ====
Native merchants from [[Sumatra]] and the [[Malay Peninsula]] actively traded in Penang following the establishment of [[George Town, Penang|George Town]]. Malay merchants traded rattan, agricultural produce such as sago, rice, pepper, spices, ivory, ebony, tin and gold, in exchange for European goods.<ref name="Keat Gin-2015" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Hussin |first=Nordin |date=Dec 2005 |title=Networks of Malay Merchants and the Rise of Penang as a Regional Trading Centre |url=https://repository.kulib.kyoto-u.ac.jp/dspace/bitstream/2433/53825/1/KJ00004062910.pdf |journal=Southeast Asian Studies |volume=43 |issue=3}}</ref> On the island, Malays originally resided at the outskirts of the new settlement, such as at the [[Pinang River (Penang)|Pinang River]], Jalan Perak, [[Dato Keramat Road, George Town|Dato Keramat Road]], [[Batu Uban]] and Teluk Duyung.<ref name="Keat Gin-2015" /> By 1798, a "Malay town" had emerged to the south of Acheen Street.<ref>{{Cite book |last=De Bierre |first=Julia |title=Penang Through Gilded Doors |publisher=Areca Books |year=2006 |isbn=9789834283421 |page=96}}</ref>
 
In Province Wellesley (now [[Seberang Perai]]), Malays were primarily engaged in rural subsistence rice farming and coastal fishing. The [[Siamese invasion of Kedah|Siamese invasion of neighbouring Kedah]] in 1821 forced an influx of Malay refugees into Province Wellesley, leading to an increase in the mainland territory's population to approximatelt 67,000 by 1858.<ref name="Keat Gin-2015" />
 
Apart from indigenous Malays, Penang also attracted immigrants from Sumatra and Java.<ref name=":0" /> Pepper trade drew in merchants from Aceh, which gradually assimilated with the local Malay community through commercial ties and intermarriages. Acehnese prominence in the pepper trade led to the emergence of a Malay Muslim entrepreneurial enclave centred at Acheen Street. Meanwhile, early Javanese settlers in Penang were engaged as workers in the spice and sugar plantations in Province Wellesley, as well as at the Eastern Smelting Company, George Town's sole tin smelting company. Dutch restrictions limited Javanese immigration to Penang, and the Javanese community in the colony was similarly assimilated into the wider Malay group.<ref name="Keat Gin-2015" />
 
Local academics and politicians allege that in the decades following [[Federation of Malaya|Malaya]]'s independence, rapid development and rising living costs have resulted in the displacement of ethnic Malays from the [[Central George Town, Penang|city centre of George Town]] to mainland [[Seberang Perai]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite news |last=Carolyn K |date=9 Aug 2024 |title=Penang 'wakaf' land can quell fears of Malay displacement, says expert |url=https://www.freemalaysiatoday.com/category/nation/2024/08/09/penang-wakaf-land-can-quell-fears-of-malay-displacement-says-expert/ |access-date=9 Aug 2024 |work=[[Free Malaysia Today]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Palanisamy |first=Ramasamy |author-link=Ramasamy Palanisamy |date=29 Jul 2024 |title=Housing project for Penang Malays attractive, but the devil is in the detail |url=https://www.freemalaysiatoday.com/category/opinion/2024/07/29/housing-project-for-penang-malays-attractive-but-the-devils-in-the-detail/ |access-date=9 Aug 2024 |work=[[Free Malaysia Today]]}}</ref> By 1975, the majority of the land within the city centre was estimated to be owned by [[Penangite Chinese|ethnic Chinese]].<ref name=":3" /> This led to underlying communal tensions, with Malay organisations such as the [[United Malays National Organisation]] (UMNO) and the Penang Malays Association (Pemenang) aggressively advocating for development initiatives specifically tailored to Malays.<ref name="Jenkins-2008">{{Cite book |last=Jenkins |first=Gwynn |title=Contested Space: Cultural Heritage and Identity Reconstructions : Conservation Strategies Within a Developing Asian City |publisher=LIT Verlag Münster |year=2008 |isbn=9783825813666}}</ref> Proposals have been made to establish a Malay enclave within downtown George Town, raising concerns about potential shifts in voting patterns.<ref name=":4" />

==== Indian ====
{{See also|Malaysians of Indian descent in Penang}}
[[File:Thaipusam Festival The Golden Chariot and the Followers.jpg|thumb|In [[George Town, Penang|George Town]], [[Thaipusam]] is celebrated with processions taking place throughout the city.]]
Convicts from the [[Indian subcontinent]] were brought to Penang soon after the founding of [[George Town, Penang|George Town]] for public works. The transfer of convicts to Penang increased with the designation of Penang as a penal station in 1795, replacing [[Port Blair]] in the [[Andaman Islands]]. These arrivals were joined by soldiers from [[Chennai|Madras]] {{Ndash}} both Hindu and Muslim {{Ndash}} who were deployed as Penang's garrison force. Commercial links with the Indian subcontinent also attracted merchants and labourers from Mumbai and [[Coromandel Coast|Coromandel]] to Penang; the south Indian Muslim traders from the latter were referred to as “Chuliahs” by [[Francis Light]] himself.<ref name="Keat Gin-2015" />
 
North Indian arrivals included [[Bengalis]], [[Parsis|Parsees]], [[Punjabis]], [[Sindhis]] and [[Gujarati people|Gujeratis]]. The northern Indians and Indian Muslims were prominently involved in wholesaling, retail and distribution trade. However, the [[Tamil Malaysians|Tamils]] of southern India soon formed the bulk of the Indian community in Penang. Tamils primarily worked as labourers, stevedores, plantation workers and in petty trading. Money lending also became the forte of the “[[chettiar]]”, a Hindu clan.<ref name="Keat Gin-2015" />
 
George Town has long been a home to the distinct [[Jawi Peranakan]] community, which descended from intermarriages between Indians and local Malay womenfolk, particularly from [[Kedah Sultanate|Kedah]]. The Jawi Peranakan traditionally dominated in money changing, jewellery, newspaper distribution, publishing, petty trading, and bakery and bread distributions. Staple dishes of the Jawi Peranakans such as [[nasi kandar]] and [[mee goreng]] have become among the more popular foods in Penang to this day.<ref name="Keat Gin-2015" />

==== Eurasian ====
Penang is home to a small [[Kristang people|Eurasian]] community, largely clustered around [[Kampong Serani|Kampung Serani]] in [[George Town, Penang|George Town]]. Descended from intermarriages between Europeans and Asians, Eurasians made up among the earliest immigrants to Penang; in 1786, soon after the establishment of George Town, a group of Eurasians from [[Kuala Kedah]] settled at China Street and Bishop Street. In the 1910s, another community of Eurasians from [[Phuket (city)|Phuket]] settled at what is now Kampung Serani.<ref name="Keat Gin-2015" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Maria Jolly |first=Ione |date=Aug 2017 |title=Identity, Community and Place: The Post-World War II Eurasian Exodus from Malaysia and Singapore to Australia |url=https://ris.cdu.edu.au/ws/portalfiles/portal/22706809/Thesis_CDU_61437_Jolly_I.pdf |journal=[[Charles Darwin University]]}}</ref> Those of Portuguese ancestry proscribed to the Catholic faith, while those with Anglo-Dutch lineage tended to be Protestants. The Eurasians in Penang share a common affinity with the [[Peranakan Chinese]] due to their mixed ancestries and their Western-oriented educational background, which also allowed the Eurasians to serve in clerical positions in the colonial bureaucracy, European businesses and the professions.<ref name="Keat Gin-2015" />

==== Siamese ====
[[File:Songkran penang.jpg|thumb|Revellers celebrating [[Songkran]] at [[Wat Chayamangkalaram]] in [[George Town, Penang|George Town]].]]
[[Kampung Siam, Penang|Kampung Siam]] in [[George Town, Penang|George Town]] is an enclave established by [[Malaysian Siamese|Siamese]] immigrants, centred around [[Wat Chayamangkalaram]]. The area had been cleared in 1795 and by 1830, there were 648 Siamese and Burmese residents in the new settlement. Siamese and Burmese settlers worked in cash crop plantations and petty trade. Intermarriages were common between the two ethnicities and the [[Penangite Chinese|Chinese]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Khoo |first=Salma Nasution |date=2012 |title=Exploring Shared History, Preserving Shared Heritage: Penang's Links to a Siamese Past |url=https://thesiamsociety.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/04/JSS_100_0s_Khoo_ExploringSharedHistoryPreservingSharedHeritagePenangsLinksToASiamesePast.pdf |journal=[[Siam Society]] |volume=100 |pages=295–322}}</ref>
 
The close links between Siam and Penang were retained into the 20th century. In 1915, [[Vajiravudh|King Rama VI]] visited George Town, during which he laid the foundation stone of the [[Kek Lok Si]]'s pagoda. In 1962, [[Bhumibol Adulyadej|King Bhumibol Adulyadej]] unveiled the Reclining Buddha statue within Wat Chayamangkalaram, in a ceremony attended by thousands of local residents.<ref name=":1" /> To this day, [[Thailand]] maintains a consulate at [[Pulau Tikus]], within the vicinity of Kampung Siam.<ref>{{Cite news |last=B. |first=Kathy |date=12 Mar 2021 |title=The former residence of the first prime minister of Malaysia is on the market for RM62 million |url=https://www.nst.com.my/property/2021/03/673165/former-residence-first-prime-minister-malaysia-market-rm62-million |access-date=2 Aug 2024 |work=[[New Straits Times]]}}</ref>

== Religion ==
{{Bar chart|title=Religions in Penang in 2020{{my10|2020kf}}|label_type=Religion|data_type=Population|label1=[[Islam]]|data1=792187|label2=[[Buddhism]]|data2=654808|label3=[[Hinduism]]|data3=145871|label4=[[Christianity]]|data4=75345|label5=Other|data5=42025|label6=[[Irreligion|No religion]]|data6=30169|label11=Total|data11=1740405|data_max=1740405}}
{{multiple image
| perrow            = 2
| total_width       = 300
| align             = right
| image1            = Penang Malaysia Sunrise at Tanjong Bungah Mosque-04and (4461552447).jpg
| image2            = Kek Lok Si at dusk.jpg
| image3            = A Hindu temple in Penang Malaysia.jpg
| image4            = Cmglee Penang Anglican church night.jpg
| footer            = Clockwise from top left: [[Penang Floating Mosque|Tanjong Bungah Floating Mosque]], [[Kek Lok Si]], [[St. George's Church, Penang|St. George's Church]] and  [[Arulmigu Karumariamman Temple]]
}}
[[Islam]] is the official religion in Penang, prescribed by over 45% of the state's population in 2020.{{my10|2020kf}}<ref name="Penang State Gov" /> Penang is one of only two states where Islam is not in the majority, the other being [[Sarawak]]. Non-Muslims collectively formed almost 55% of Penang's population.{{my10|2020kf}}
 
[[Buddhism]] is the second most proscribed religion in Penang, with nearly 37% of the population being adherents of either [[Theravada]], [[Mahayana]] or [[Vajrayana]] sects.{{my10|2020kf}} Notably, Theravada Buddhism is influenced by various countries of origin, with Thai, Burmese and Sinhalese temples established throughout George Town since the colonial era.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Woon Khin |first=Benny Liow |date=1989 |title=Buddhist Temples and Associations in Penang, 1845–1948 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41493627 |journal=[[Malaysian Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society]] |volume=62 |issue=1 |pages=57–87 |jstor=41493627 }}</ref> [[Hinduism|Hindus]] made up the third largest religion in Penang, at over 8%, followed by the [[Christianity|Christians]] at 4%.{{my10|2020kf}} The first [[Kristang people|Eurasian]] settlers in George Town brought along [[Catholic Church|Catholicism]], while small numbers of missionaries from the [[London Missionary Society]] sought to evangelise the non-Christian population into Protestanism. Both sects also established some of George Town's oldest [[mission school]]s, including [[St. Xavier's Institution|St Xavier's Institution]], [[Convent Light Street]] and [[St. George's Girls' School]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cho |first=Young Mook |date=Mar 2022 |title=Formation process of Chinese Community in Penang, 1786–1830 |url=https://etheses.whiterose.ac.uk/31497/1/Cho_YM_History_PhD_2022.pdf |journal=[[University of Leeds]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Hollen Lees |first=Lynn |title=Planting Empire, Cultivating Subjects |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |year=2017 |isbn=9781107038400 |page=146}}</ref>
 
The [[Government of Penang|Penang state government]] maintains a policy of freedom of religion and religious assembly, and is also one of only three states in Malaysia to have a dedicated department for non-Muslim affairs.<ref name="Penang State Gov" /><ref name="Opalyn Mok-2023">{{Cite news |last=Opalyn Mok |date=25 Dec 2023 |title=Kon Yeow: Penang Allocates RM10m for Development of Non-Islamic Places of Worship until 2028 |url=https://www.malaymail.com/news/malaysia/2023/12/25/kon-yeow-penang-allocates-rm10m-for-development-of-non-islamic-places-of-worship-until-2028/109143 |access-date=17 Mar 2024 |work=[[Malay Mail]]}}</ref> In 2021, the state government formed the Penang Harmony Corporation to further enhance interreligious harmony in the state.<ref name="Opalyn Mok-20232">{{Cite news |last=Opalyn Mok |date=25 Dec 2023 |title=Kon Yeow: Penang Allocates RM10m for Development of Non-Islamic Places of Worship until 2028 |url=https://www.malaymail.com/news/malaysia/2023/12/25/kon-yeow-penang-allocates-rm10m-for-development-of-non-islamic-places-of-worship-until-2028/109143 |access-date=17 Mar 2024 |work=[[Malay Mail]]}}</ref> In particular, [[Pitt Street, George Town|Pitt Street]], within [[Central George Town, Penang|George Town]]'s [[George Town Central Business District, Penang|Central Business District]] (CBD), houses multiple places of worship belonging to Muslim, Taoist, Hindu and Christian communities, all located in close proximity to each other. This unique arrangement has earned Pitt Street the nickname "Street of Harmony".<ref>{{Cite book |last=[[Christian Giordano]] |title=De Palerme À Penang |publisher=[[LIT Verlag]] |year=2010 |isbn=978-3-643-80062-6}}</ref>

== Languages ==
[[File:Victoria_St,_George_Town,_Penang.jpg|thumb|A bilingual street sign in [[George Town, Penang|George Town]]. Bilingual street signs that display either [[British English|English]], [[Chinese language|Chinese]], [[Tamil language|Tamil]] or [[Arabic]] names have been installed throughout the city since 2008.<ref name="Ng-2008">{{Cite news |last=Ng |first=Su-Ann |date=22 November 2008 |title=Multilingual Road Signs Put Up to Boost Penang's Tourism |url=https://www.thestar.com.my/news/nation/2008/11/22/multilingual-road-signs-put-up-to-boost-penangs-tourism/ |work=[[The Star (Malaysia)|The Star]]}}</ref>]]
In Penang's diverse urban community, [[Malay language|Malay]], [[British English|English]], [[Hokkien]], [[Malaysian Mandarin|Mandarin]], and [[Malaysian Tamil|Tamil]] are commonly used languages.<ref name="Teresa Wai-20223"/> Penang is particularly renowned for its unique [[Penang Hokkien]] dialect.<ref name="Opalyn Mok-2016-122">{{Cite news |last=Opalyn Mok |date=2 August 2016 |title=Penang Hokkien Will Be 'Dead' in 40 years If People Stop Using It, Says Language Expert |url=https://www.malaymail.com/news/malaysia/2016/08/02/penang-hokkien-will-be-dead-in-40-years-if-people-stop-using-it-says-langua/1174401 |work=[[Malay Mail]]}}</ref>
 
Like the rest of Malaysia, Malay is the official language in Penang. The [[Jawi Peranakan]]s in the state also use a variant of the [[Kedah Malay]] dialect, slightly modified to suit the conditions of a cosmopolitan society.<ref name="Rahim-2015">{{Cite journal |last=Abdul Rahim |first=Hajar |date=2015 |title=Bahasa Tanjong: The Heritage Language of the Jawi Peranakans of Penang |url=http://web.usm.my/km/33(Supp.2)2015/km33s22015_06.pdf |journal=Kajian Malaysia |volume=33}}</ref>
 
English had been the official language in Penang during British rule. The growth of English and [[Mission School|mission schools]] throughout [[George Town, Penang|George Town]] contributed significantly to the widespread use of the language in the state.<ref name="Ooi-2015">{{Cite journal |last=Ooi |first=Keat Gin |date=2015 |title=Disparate Identities: Penang from a Historical Perspective, 1780–1941 |url=http://web.usm.my/km/33(Supp.2)2015/km33s22015_03.pdf |journal=Kajian Malaysia |volume=33 |issue=Supp. 2 |pages=27–52 |issn=0127-4082 |access-date=2023-03-07 |df=dmy-all}}</ref> The importance of English for global trade has also encouraged its adoption by the [[Penangite Chinese|Chinese]] and [[Malaysians of Indian descent in Penang|Indian]] communities.<ref name="Teresa Wai-20223"/> In recent years, there have been calls to reinstate English as one of Penang's official languages.<ref>{{Cite news |date=8 Nov 2010 |title=Penang Backbencher Proposes English as State's Second Official Language |url=https://www.thestar.com.my/news/nation/2010/11/08/penang-backbencher-proposes-english-as-states-second-official-language |access-date=5 Dec 2023 |work=[[The Star (Malaysia)|The Star]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=20 Jun 2022 |title=Penang Should Make English Second Language Like Sarawak, Says PKR Rep |url=https://www.freemalaysiatoday.com/category/nation/2022/06/20/penang-should-make-english-second-language-like-sarawak-says-pkr-rep/ |access-date=5 Dec 2023 |work=[[Free Malaysia Today]]}}</ref>
 
[[Tamil language|Tamil]] is the most widely spoken language amongst ethnic Indians. In addition to Tamil, the other Indian languages used by minority Indians are [[Telugu language|Telugu]] and [[Punjabi language|Punjabi]], who hailed from diverse ancestries in the [[Indian subcontinent]].<ref name="Ooi-2015" /><ref>{{Cite web |date=May 2017 |title=Dialects and Languages in Numbers |url=http://penangmonthly.com/article.aspx?pageid=7447&name=dialects_and_languages_in_numbers |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170516160537/http://www.penangmonthly.com/article.aspx?pageid=7447&name=dialects_and_languages_in_numbers |archive-date=16 May 2017 |access-date=27 May 2017 |website=Penang Monthly}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Lin |first=Rouwen |date=3 October 2010 |title=The Telugu Heritage |url=https://www.thestar.com.my/lifestyle/features/2010/10/03/the-telugu-heritage/ |work=[[The Star (Malaysia)|The Star]]}}</ref> On the other hand, Penang's Chinese population uses a variety of Chinese dialects, including [[Teochew Chinese|Teochew]], [[Hakka Chinese|Hakka]] and [[Cantonese]].<ref name="Ooi-2015" /><ref name="Teresa Wai-20223" /> [[Mandarin Chinese|Mandarin]], which is more commonly used by youths for pragmatic reasons, has been the medium of instruction in Chinese schools throughout the state.<ref name="Ooi Kok Hin"/>
 
Penang Hokkien serves as the ''[[lingua franca]]'' between the various ethnicities in Penang.<ref name="Opalyn Mok-2016-122"/><ref>{{Cite web |last=Qi |first=Koh Aun |date=9 September 2017 |title=Penang and its struggle for survival |url=https://newnaratif.com/journalism/penang-hokkien-and-its-struggle-for-survival/ |access-date=17 February 2021 |work=New Naratif}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Ann Tan |date=30 July 2009 |title=Mind your Hokkien |url=https://www.thestar.com.my/news/community/2009/07/30/mind-your-hokkien/ |work=[[The Star (Malaysia)|The Star]]}}</ref> Originally a variant of the [[Southern Min]] group of languages, the dialect has absorbed numerous loanwords from Malay and English, yet another legacy of the [[Peranakan Chinese]] culture. Community efforts have been made to preserve the relevance of Penang Hokkien in the face of the rising prevalence of Mandarin and English among youths.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Bernard Cheah |date=17 August 2016 |title=Translating Penang Hokkien to English with ease |url=https://thesun.my/archive/1939512-GSARCH388293 |work=[[The Sun (Malaysia)|The Sun]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last= |date=7 Jul 2023 |title=Learn to Speak Hokkien Like a True Penangite |url=https://www.thestar.com.my/news/nation/2023/07/07/learn-to-speak-hokkien-like-a-true-penangite |access-date=5 Dec 2023 |work=[[The Star (Malaysia)|The Star]]}}</ref>
 
== Age distribution ==
{{As of|2020}}, Penang was the second “oldest” state in the country after [[Perak]]. 14.9% of Penang's population were aged 60 and older, and it was anticipated that the state will have the highest proportion of residents over 60s in Malaysia by 2040.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Pfordten |first=Diyana |date=22 Jan 2020 |title=Malaysia's states set to rapidly age as they fail to retain young talent |url=https://www.scmp.com/news/asia/southeast-asia/article/3047100/malaysias-states-set-rapidly-age-they-fail-retain-young |access-date=2 Aug 2024 |work=[[South China Morning Post]]}}</ref> The state and local governments have begun formulating age-friendly policies to support a rapidly ageing population, including more inclusive infrastructure, improving access to healthcare and encouraging [[active ageing]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yeong |first1=Pey Jung |last2=Chan |first2=Xin Ying |date=28 Oct 2022 |title=A Sustainable Active Ageing Policy for Penang |url=https://penanginstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/A-Sustainable-Active-Ageing-Policy-for-Penang.pdf |journal=Penang Institute}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date= |title=Age Friendly City |url=https://www.mbpp.gov.my/en/services/bandar-mesra-usia?showall=1 |access-date=2 Aug 2024 |website=[[Penang Island City Council]]}}</ref>
